scenarios.title: Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.brief: A meal-kit company runs a customer support agent on the Claude Agent SDK. Its MCP tools are get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human and pause_subscription. The agent may refund up to $150 per box; larger refunds go to a human.

scenarios.title: Scenario 2 — Code Generation with Claude Code
scenarios.brief: A startup uses Claude Code in one TypeScript repository with server/, mobile/ and packages/shared/ folders. The repository commits a .claude/ directory and a root CLAUDE.md. Engineers use Claude Code to generate endpoints, screens and tests from tickets.

scenarios.title: Scenario 6 — Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.brief: An insurance broker extracts data from certificates of insurance sent by many carriers. Claude returns the insured name, carrier, policy number, limits, deductibles and dates through a tool with a JSON schema. A validator checks each result before it is posted to the broker's system.

questions.question: Customers who want to cancel are handed to a person through escalate_to_human. Product would like the agent to suggest pausing the subscription first, before it hands the customer over. This is a retention idea, not a business rule, so the agent does not have to do it in every chat. What is the most appropriate way to add it?

options.t: Add a system-prompt instruction to suggest a pause, plus two short example chats.
options.why: Best. A soft behaviour, where an occasional miss does no harm, is what prompt guidance is for. One instruction and two examples are easy to maintain.

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks escalate_to_human until a pause has been offered.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. The hook would make the offer happen every time, but it needs code to spot cancellations and track what was said. Guarantees are for business rules.

options.t: Add the pause offer to the escalate_to_human description, so Claude offers it before calling the tool.
options.why: Works, but wrong home. Claude does read tool descriptions, but they explain when and how to call a tool. How to talk to the customer belongs in the system prompt, where it is easy to find and change.

options.t: Route every cancellation request to a new retention subagent before it reaches a human.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. A retention subagent could make the offer well, but it adds a handoff and another prompt to maintain, for one sentence of behaviour.

questions.decider: This is a retention idea, not a business rule, so the agent does not have to do it in every chat.
questions.explanation: Programmatic enforcement is for steps that must happen every time. A best-effort suggestion is shaped with a clear instruction plus a few examples.

eli5.question: Product wants the agent to ask “would you like to pause instead?” before it hands a cancellation to a person. The clue: it's a retention idea, not a business rule.
eli5.answer: A shop asks staff to mention the loyalty card at the till. A note and a quick demo do the job; nobody installs a till that locks until the card is mentioned. Here the note is a system-prompt instruction and the demo is example chats. Rule: must happen every time → code. Nice to have → prompt and examples.
options: Correct. A plain instruction plus examples sets the nudge.
A lock in code (a hook) is for things that must never be skipped. Here skipping is allowed.
Tool instructions would work, but they're the wrong place for how to talk to customers.
A whole new helper agent for one friendly sentence is too much.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the most reliable option is always the best one. The question asks for the most appropriate one. Code-level enforcement (a hook) is right when a step must happen every time, such as checking identity before a refund. For a nice-to-have it is extra machinery: something has to detect cancellations and remember what was said.
deep.diagram:
Must it happen every time?
  yes → hook or prerequisite gate (code)
  no  → prompt instruction + examples
deep.mapTitle: How firmly must this behaviour hold?

head: Situation
Right mechanism
Why
rows: A suggestion or tone; an occasional miss is harmless
A business rule; a miss costs money or breaks policy
Hook or prerequisite gate in code
Prompts have a non-zero failure rate
Sensitive data must never reach the model
The model can't repeat what it never saw
Guidance on when and how to call a tool
Claude reads it when choosing tools
Instructions are clear but output still varies

evidence.quote: Product would like the agent to suggest pausing the subscription first, before it hands the customer over
evidence.means: The goal is a suggestion in the conversation. That belongs in Claude's instructions, not in a tool's description ([[2]]).

evidence.quote: This is a retention idea, not a business rule, so the agent does not have to do it in every chat
evidence.means: The decider. Missing it now and then is harmless, so a hook ([[1]]) or a new subagent ([[3]]) is more than the goal needs.

evidence.quote: What is the most appropriate way to add it?
evidence.means: “Most appropriate” means the right size: an instruction with examples, [[0]].

deep.rule: Business rule → enforce it in code. Suggestion or style → prompt instruction plus examples.

guide.obj: 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
guide.quote: Programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) vs prompt-based guidance.

questions.question: Customers usually describe a box by when it arrived, for example “last Tuesday's box”. The agent passes that date to lookup_order as the box ID, and the call fails. Each customer's box IDs are listed in their get_customer record. The description of lookup_order is one line: “Looks up a box.” What is the most effective first step?

options.t: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt that turn a delivery date into a box ID first.
options.why: Works, but leaves the cause in place. Examples would teach the date-to-ID step, but they add tokens to every request while the one-line description stays unclear. They are a later step.

options.t: Add a routing layer that detects dates and calls get_customer before lookup_order.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt for a first step. Code that spots dates and calls get_customer first would fix this case, but it is fragile and far more work than a better description.

options.t: Expand the lookup_order description with the ID format, an example, and where IDs come from.
options.why: Best. Claude learns how to call a tool mainly from its description. This one gives no ID format and no route from a date to an ID, and fixing that is cheap.

options.t: Add a lookup_order_by_date tool that takes a delivery date and returns the box.
options.why: Works, but more than a first step. A date-based tool would handle this request, but it is new code, and with equally thin descriptions the agent can misuse it too.

questions.decider: The description of lookup_order is one line: “Looks up a box.”
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the main signal for how to call a tool. A minimal description should first be expanded with input format, examples, edge cases and boundaries.

eli5.question: The agent keeps putting a date where a box ID should go. The clue: the tool's instructions are four words long.
eli5.answer: If a form field just says “Box”, people write all sorts of things in it. Write “Box ID, like BX-20431, found on the customer record” and most mistakes stop. For Claude, the tool description is that label. Rule: tool misused and its description is thin → fix the description first.
options: Examples help later, but the label itself is still unclear.
A program that hunts for dates in messages is a lot of work for a first step.
Correct. Fix the label: say what an ID looks like and where to find it.
A second tool with an equally vague label can go wrong the same way.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the agent needs more examples or smarter routing. But Claude decides how to call a tool mainly from the tool's description. “Looks up a box” gives no ID format and no hint that IDs come from get_customer. Fix that first: it is cheap and it fixes the cause.
deep.diagram:
"Looks up a box" → Claude guesses → date as ID → fail
+ ID format, example, where IDs come from → right call
deep.mapTitle: A tool is called wrongly. What do you fix first?

head: What you observe
Where the fault is
First fix
rows: Wrong input passed; the description is one line
Two similar tools get mixed up
Descriptions are detailed; behaviour still varies
Agent prefers Grep over a better MCP tool
Bad calls happen and the agent can't recover
Structured error naming the expected format

evidence.quote: Customers usually describe a box by when it arrived
evidence.means: The agent gets a date, so the tool must explain how to get from a date to an ID.

evidence.quote: The agent passes that date to lookup_order as the box ID, and the call fails
evidence.means: The agent doesn't know what a box ID looks like. That is a description problem, not a routing problem ([[1]]).

evidence.quote: Each customer's box IDs are listed in their get_customer record
evidence.means: The data to fix it already exists. The agent just isn't told where to look, which a description can say.

evidence.quote: The description of lookup_order is one line: “Looks up a box.”
evidence.means: The decider. The cause is a thin description, so examples ([[0]]) and a new tool ([[3]]) work around it.

evidence.quote: What is the most effective first step?
evidence.means: First step = the cheapest change that fixes the cause: [[2]].

deep.rule: A tool gets the wrong input and its description is thin? Expand the description first.

guide.obj: 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries
guide.quote: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for selection

questions.question: The team's accessibility conventions apply to every screen file. Screen files are named *.screen.tsx and live in mobile/ and packages/shared/ui/. The conventions sit in the root CLAUDE.md, so they also load during server work. Where should they go?

options.t: A CLAUDE.md in mobile/, and one in packages/shared/ui/ that imports it.
options.why: Works, but tied to folders. Folder CLAUDE.md files would load the conventions for screens, but they need one per tree and also load for every other file in those folders.

options.t: An /a11y skill that engineers invoke when they work on a screen.
options.why: Works, but only when someone remembers. A skill loads when it is invoked, so screens edited without it miss the conventions.

options.t: A file in .claude/rules/ whose paths: frontmatter is **/*.screen.tsx.
options.why: Best. A path-scoped rule loads whenever Claude edits a matching file, in any folder, and stays out of server work.

options.t: A separate markdown file pulled into the root CLAUDE.md with an @import line.
options.why: Works, but still loads everywhere. @import keeps the conventions in their own file, which is tidier, but they still load in every session, including server work.

questions.decider: Screen files … live in mobile/ and packages/shared/ui/.
questions.explanation: Conventions tied to a file type that spans folders belong in .claude/rules/ with a paths glob. They load only for matching files, wherever those files are.

eli5.question: Some rules apply only to screen files, which sit in two different folders. Right now Claude reads those rules even when it works on the server.
eli5.answer: Picture a sticky note that pops up only when you open a certain kind of file, wherever it is. That's a rule file with a path pattern in .claude/rules/. A folder CLAUDE.md is a note stuck on a folder: fine when everything is in one folder, clumsy when the files are spread out. Rule: convention follows a file pattern → path-scoped rule. Convention follows a folder → folder CLAUDE.md.
options: Notes stuck on two folders: copies to keep in sync, and they show up for other files in those folders too.
A skill waits until someone asks for it. People forget.
Correct. The note appears for screen files only, in any folder.
Importing into the root file still loads it for everyone, every time.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think conventions belong in a CLAUDE.md near the code. That works when the code sits in one folder. These conventions follow a file name pattern across two trees. Claude Code can load a rule file only when the file being edited matches a glob, wherever it lives.
deep.diagram:
.claude/rules/a11y.md   paths: **/*.screen.tsx
  mobile/home.screen.tsx          → loaded
  packages/shared/ui/x.screen.tsx → loaded
  server/api.ts                   → not loaded

head: Where it applies
Best home
Why
rows: Files matching a pattern, in many folders
Loads by file, in any folder
Shared with the team through git
A task someone runs on request

evidence.quote: The team's accessibility conventions apply to every screen file
evidence.means: The convention follows a kind of file, which is what a paths: glob matches.

evidence.quote: Screen files are named *.screen.tsx and live in mobile/ and packages/shared/ui/
evidence.means: The decider. Two trees, so folder CLAUDE.md files ([[0]]) need a copy per tree.

evidence.quote: The conventions sit in the root CLAUDE.md, so they also load during server work
evidence.means: The goal is to stop loading them everywhere. An @import from the root ([[3]]) still loads everywhere.

evidence.quote: Where should they go?
evidence.means: A rule that loads by itself for matching files: [[2]]. A skill ([[1]]) needs someone to invoke it.

deep.rule: Convention follows a file pattern across folders → .claude/rules/ with a paths glob.

guide.obj: 3.3 Path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
guide.quote: Glob-pattern rules beat directory CLAUDE.md for conventions spanning directories

questions.question: Many certificates do not show a deductible at all. In the schema, deductible is a required number. For these certificates, the extraction returns 0 or copies the coverage limit into the field. Those values are posted as if they were printed, and reviewers cannot tell them apart from real ones. What is the best fix?

options.t: Add two example certificates with no deductible to the prompt, each with its expected output.
options.why: Works, but only partly. Examples show what to do when no deductible is printed, but while the schema demands a number the model has no honest value to return.

options.t: Make deductible nullable in the schema, and state in its description when to return null.
options.why: Best. A required number forces the model to invent one. A nullable field gives it an honest way to say “not printed”.

options.t: Keep deductible required and have the model enter -1 whenever no deductible is printed.
options.why: Works, but fragile. -1 marks the gap, but it is still a number: every system downstream must know the convention, or -1 posts as a real value.

options.t: Add a deductible_printed flag beside the number, and have reviewers ignore the number when it is false.
options.why: Works, but the invented number stays. The flag tells reviewers to ignore it, but the required field still puts a made-up value in the record, where other systems can use it.

questions.decider: In the schema, deductible is a required number.
questions.explanation: Required fields push the model to invent values when the source lacks them. Optional or nullable fields, with a description of when to leave them empty, prevent that.

eli5.question: When a certificate has no deductible, the extraction makes one up (0, or the limit). The clue: the schema says the field must always hold a number.
eli5.answer: A form with a box that must contain a number, and no “not applicable” option, makes people write something, anything. Add “leave blank if not printed” and the made-up values stop. In a JSON schema that's a nullable field. Rule: the model invents values when the schema leaves it no honest answer. Make missing values nullable.
options: Showing examples doesn't help while the form still has no blank option.
Correct. Let the field be empty when nothing is printed.
-1 is still a number someone can mistake for a real one.
A “please ignore” sticker helps, but the made-up number is still on the form.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think made-up values are a prompting problem. Here the schema causes them: a required number has no valid way to say “not printed”, so the model fills it. Fix the schema first; examples help only once the schema allows an honest answer.
deep.diagram:
required number + nothing printed → model invents 0
nullable number + nothing printed → null (honest)
deep.mapTitle: Extraction output is wrong. Schema, prompt or retry?

head: What you observe
Cause
Fix
rows: Values invented when the source lacks them
Categories forced into the nearest option
Field allows null but the model still guesses
Unclear when to leave it empty
Describe the rule and add examples
A value fails a validation check

evidence.quote: Many certificates do not show a deductible at all
evidence.means: Missing is a normal case, so the output needs a way to say so.

evidence.quote: In the schema, deductible is a required number
evidence.means: The decider: the schema forces a number. Examples ([[0]]) can't fix a schema with no honest answer, and a flag ([[3]]) leaves the invented number in the record.

evidence.quote: Those values are posted as if they were printed, and reviewers cannot tell them apart from real ones
evidence.means: Invented values look real. A marker like -1 ([[2]]) has the same problem.

evidence.quote: What is the best fix?
evidence.means: Change the schema: [[1]].

deep.rule: Model inventing values for missing data? Make the field nullable and say when to use null.

questions.question: Some refund disputes go on for a long time. When a chat gets close to the context limit, the SDK replaces older turns with a summary. After that, the agent sometimes offers a smaller refund than it promised earlier. It also forgets which items the customer said were missing. Which change best fixes this?

options.t: Before each refund offer, have the agent call lookup_order again to reload the order and its items.
options.why: Works, but only for what the order system knows. It reloads the order, but the promised amount and the items the customer reported missing were said in the chat, not stored there.

options.t: Raise the threshold for summarising older turns, so more of each chat stays word for word.
options.why: Works, but only delays it. More of each chat stays word for word, but long disputes still cross the threshold and the same facts get blurred.

options.t: Tell the summariser to quote every amount and item mentioned in the earlier turns.
options.why: Works, but still lossy. A careful summary keeps most amounts, but the facts go through a summary on every pass, and each pass can drop or change them.

options.t: Keep a case-facts block of promised amounts, missing items and order IDs in every request.
options.why: Best. Facts kept outside the summarised history survive every summary, and the agent sees them on every turn.

questions.decider: After that, the agent sometimes offers a smaller refund than it promised earlier.
questions.explanation: Summarising blurs numbers, dates and promises. Pull them into a persistent case-facts block that is sent with every request instead of being summarised.

eli5.question: To save space, old parts of the chat get squeezed into a summary. After that, the agent forgets what it promised. The clue: the facts get lost in the summary.
eli5.answer: When a long meeting is summarised, exact numbers get rounded off. A good assistant keeps a separate card with the key facts: “promised $40 credit; salmon and rice missing”. The summary can be rough; the card stays exact. That card is a case-facts block sent with every request. Rule: numbers and promises that must survive go in a facts block, not the summary.
options: Re-reading the order helps, but the promises were made in the chat, not in the order.
Summarising later only moves the problem further down the chat.
A better summary is still a summary; numbers can still slip.
Correct. Keep the key facts on a separate card that never gets summarised.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a better summary will keep the facts. But every summary is a lossy step, and a long chat gets summarised again and again. Exact facts such as amounts, items and promises should not depend on a summary at all. Keep them in a separate block that goes with every request.
deep.diagram:
older turns   → summary (blurry)     ┐
case facts: $40 credit, salmon      ├→ every request
recent turns  (word for word)       ┘
deep.mapTitle: Facts go missing in a long session. Where are they lost?

head: What you observe
Cause
Fix
rows: Promised amounts or items drift after summarising
Context fills fast with long tool output
Trim results to the needed fields
Details in the middle of a long input are missed
Key facts first, clear section headers
Claims lose their sources after summarising
Keep the source with each claim

evidence.quote: When a chat gets close to the context limit, the SDK replaces older turns with a summary
evidence.means: Facts from early turns now exist only inside summaries.

evidence.quote: After that, the agent sometimes offers a smaller refund than it promised earlier
evidence.means: The decider. The loss starts after summarising, so the summary is the cause. Reloading the order ([[0]]) doesn't bring back what was promised in the chat.

evidence.quote: It also forgets which items the customer said were missing
evidence.means: More than one kind of fact is lost, so a better summary prompt ([[2]]) or a later threshold ([[1]]) only reduces or delays it.

evidence.quote: Which change best fixes this?
evidence.means: Take the facts out of the summarised history: [[3]].

deep.rule: Exact facts that must survive a long chat go into a case-facts block, not into summaries.

guide.obj: 5.1 Preserve critical information across long interactions
guide.quote: Extract transactional facts into a persistent "case facts" block
